extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political philosophy, social science, and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for choosing and judging methods in social science (political philosophy, sociology, political economy): contrasts between 'chemical', 'geometrical', and 'concrete deductive' methods and guidance on verification, scope, and appropriate compartmentalization of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical Method (avoid for complex social phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Chemical Method' is the gross misconception that one can determine causes in political phenomena by isolating and subtracting effects as in simple experimental chemistry; it assumes we can subtract the effect of all causes except one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on attempting to isolate a single cause by experimental subtraction in social inquiry — social phenomena involve many concurrent causes and you cannot subtract all other influences. Experimental argument in politics only verifies conclusions drawn from more general laws; overreliance on this method is inappropriate except insofar as it confirms deductions from broader principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical (Abstract) Method (do not treat society like geometry)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Geometrical' method treats social science as if it were like geometry — deducing consequences from a few self-evident premises that do not conflict with one another — implicitly assuming each social phenomenon flows from one law alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assimilating social science to geometry: unlike geometry, social phenomena involve conflicting and interacting forces so that results from one principle may be modified or cancelled by others. Beware systems that explain society by a single driving principle (e.g., government founded on fear, or that men's actions are always determined by private interest) — such single-factor deductions are unscientific when presented as complete theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete/Deductive Method (prefer deduction from many premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Social science should be deductive but not after the model of geometry — rather after the model of more complex physical sciences (astronomy, natural philosophy): deductions must compound the laws of multiple causes ('Concrete Deductive Method').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame deductions by considering all (or many) relevant laws of human nature and compounding their effects. Recognize increased precariousness from added complexity and prepare appropriate contrivances (methods, approximations) to handle compounding tendencies. Use comparable practice from complex physical sciences as a guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification by empirical observation (essential complement to deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive conclusions must be collated with concrete phenomena or empirical laws — verification is the third essential constituent of the deductive method and the ground of confidence in concrete deductive science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not depend on a priori deduction alone: test deductions against observation. In complex cases the order may invert (derive provisional laws from experience and then connect them to principles), but concurrence between a priori reasoning and a posteriori evidence is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of prediction: deduce tendencies, not precise forecasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Sociology considered as direct deduction cannot yield positive precise predictions but only tendencies (how a cause will operate unless counteracted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that useful sociological knowledge often consists of tendencies that guide action and precaution rather than certain outcomes. Use tendencies to design circumstances with beneficial tendencies and to guard against harmful ones, recognizing uncertainty about the magnitude and exact outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for Intermixture of Laws / consensus among social elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Social phenomena are interdependent: every part of the social state influences every other (a 'consensus'), so no social phenomenon can be fully understood in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing any social fact, consider its connections to other social facts and the wider state of civilization and history. Be cautious applying conclusions from one society or period to another without reanalyzing all influencing circumstances; differences in surrounding agencies can change effects by reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope restriction for useful general propositions (limit complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because uncertainty increases rapidly with the number of concurrent causes considered, hypothetical general theorems of the science must be limited to classes of social facts principally influenced by only a few causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict direct deductive generalizations to phenomena where immediate causes predominate; for more complex aggregates, either simplify the hypothetical conditions or prefer empirical/inverse methods to obtain reliable laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify departmental separation when dominated by one class of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: A separate branch (e.g., Political Economy) is warranted when a large class of social phenomena is mainly determined, in the first resort, by one class of circumstances (e.g., pursuit of wealth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create disciplinary subdivisions only where the immediate determining causes are largely homogeneous and the effect due to that class can be usefully analyzed 'once for all'; always allow for and later adjust by the influence of other modifying circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting partial theories as complete (don't overclaim)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unphilosophical to construct a science from only a few agencies and leave others to practice or conjecture; presenting such partial constructions as comprehensive science is a methodological error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When foundations omit important agencies, do not claim comprehensive scientific status for resulting theories; either broaden the foundational premises or limit theoretical claims and explicitly acknowledge omitted influences and their potential weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base theory on unbending practical maxims or fictions (abstract right / social contract)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductions that start from practical maxims (abstract right) or from fictions (e.g., an original social contract) mistake art for science and constitute a 'petitio principii' by assuming what the theory should explain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using normative precepts or fictional constructs as primary premises for scientific explanation of social phenomena. Rules of conduct must be grounded in the theory of the subject, not used as its foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include cultural, habitual, and traditional influences in explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations of rulers' or social actors' conduct must account for habitual sentiments, prevailing modes of thought, class characteristics, inherited maxims and traditions — not solely self-interest calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining political behavior, consider multiple non-calculative motives (sense of duty, philanthropy, traditions) and the influence of social environment and predecessor practices; neglecting these leads to incomplete or misleading accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inverse (empirical-first) method where direct deduction is inapplicable
rubrics_metrics.description: In some sociological inquiries direct deduction is altogether inapplicable due to prodigious complication; in these cases best empirical laws are obtainable first, and then connected to principles by a priori reasoning (the inverse method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when complexity prevents reliable a priori deduction and instead derive provisional laws from specific experience, later integrating them with human-nature principles. Balance and alternate direct and inverse procedures according to the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat general propositions as hypothetical and context-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: All general propositions from deductive sociology are hypothetical — they assume a set of circumstances and state how a given cause would operate under those suppositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying general propositions to actual societies, verify whether the assumed circumstances match reality and perform anew the analysis if not. Increase the number of individualizing circumstances in the hypothesis for nearer concrete truth, but beware accumulating liabilities to error.
